title: Fatigue in a 23-year-old student: heavy periods and iron deficiency anaemia
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 23-year-old psychology student with 2 to 3 months of worsening fatigue in general practice. The candidate finds symptoms of anaemia and heavy menstrual bleeding and looks for the signs of iron deficiency. They then interpret her full blood count and film, iron studies and screening bloods, and plan iron replacement, treatment of the heavy bleeding, follow-up and safety netting.
focus: Fatigue in a young woman: recognising iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding, confirming it and managing both the cause and the iron deficit in general practice
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a suburban general practice. Sylvie, a 23-year-old university student, has booked an appointment because she has been feeling tired. Your GP supervisor will see her after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Sylvie and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the results of Sylvie's full blood count and blood film, iron studies and other blood tests. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Sylvie, a 23-year-old psychology student. You are tired, a bit flat and frustrated, but you speak freely. You have not linked your tiredness to your periods and do not mention them unless asked. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I am always exhausted, no matter how much I sleep."

The tiredness (give only when asked):

  • It came on gradually over the last 2 to 3 months and has got much worse in the last few weeks.
  • More sleep does not help. Any activity makes you more tired, so you have stopped exercising.
  • "I can't even concentrate in my tutes, let alone bring myself to study... I'm just so tired."

Other symptoms (give only when asked):

  • Palpitations: "I feel my heart thumping in my chest sometimes." It is regular and fast, for example when you climb the stairs.
  • Breathlessness: you get breathless going up stairs, and in the last few weeks even when walking to uni. You have never had this before.
  • Dizziness: you feel light-headed at times, especially when you stand up quickly. The room does not spin and you do not feel off-balance. You have not fainted.
  • Legs and hands: cramps in your legs when you walk. Your hands and feet are always cold.
  • No unusual cravings (if asked about chewing ice or eating odd things).

Periods (give only when asked about periods):

  • First period at 12. Periods come every 28 days.
  • Over the last year or so they have become longer: now 8 days, where they used to last 5.
  • Last period started last Tuesday.
  • You change pads and tampons every 2 hours on heavy days and get up at night to change them. On day 1 you "flood" through.
  • The blood is bright red, then darker. You often pass large clots.
  • The period pain is quite bad and you take Ponstan for it. Before your period you get a dull headache and mood swings. You have never had flashing lights, zigzag lines, numbness or trouble speaking with a headache, and you have never been told you have migraine. No blood clots in the legs or lungs in you or your family.

Negatives (only if asked):

  • No chest pain, cough or runny nose. No snoring or pauses in breathing that anyone has noticed.
  • No change in weight or appetite, no sweats or fevers, no headaches apart from before your period.
  • No tummy pain, heartburn, diarrhoea, constipation, blood in your poo or black poo. No blood in your urine.
  • No easy bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums. You have never bled a lot after a cut, a dental procedure or an operation.
  • No travel overseas. You have not given blood for years.
  • Mood: you are frustrated about uni but not depressed. You still enjoy seeing friends when you have the energy. You sleep 9 to 10 hours a night.

Sexual history (if asked): not in a relationship and not sexually active for over a year. You are not on any contraception. There is no chance you are pregnant.

Past medical history: previously well. No operations.

Medicines: Ponstan (mefenamic acid) during your periods, and a Centrum multivitamin. No contraception.

Allergies: hayfever. No drug allergies.

Family history: your mother has osteoarthritis and your father has gout. Nobody in the family has a bleeding disorder, coeliac disease or bowel cancer.

Social history:

  • Psychology student. You live with flatmates and are well supported by friends and family.
  • Non-smoker. You do not drink alcohol.
  • You eat mostly takeaway (noodles, pizza, chips) and rarely eat red meat, but you are not vegetarian.
  • You are too tired to exercise at the moment.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: maybe it is uni stress.
  • Concern: "I'm not sure what's wrong with me." You are falling behind in your studies.
  • Expectation: "I want my energy back."

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: "Do you think it's just stress from uni?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General: alert, looks pale and tired, comfortable at rest. Weight 58 kg, height 166 cm, BMI 21 kg/m².
  • Observations: HR 104/min, regular. BP 108/68 mmHg lying; standing 102/64 mmHg with HR 116/min, and she says she feels a little light-headed. RR 16/min. SpO2 99% on room air. Temperature 36.6 °C.
  • Hands: pale palmar creases. Spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia). Cool hands. Capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing.
  • Face and mouth: conjunctival pallor. Cracks at the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis). Smooth, pale, atrophic tongue (glossitis). No jaundice.
  • Skin and hair: dry skin, dry brittle hair. No bruising, petechiae or purpura.
  • Neck: no lymphadenopathy. Thyroid not enlarged, no nodules.
  • Cardiovascular: pulse regular. JVP not raised. Heart sounds dual, with a soft ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that does not radiate. No ankle oedema. Chest clear.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender. No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. No masses, and no palpable uterus or pelvic mass.
  • Pelvic examination (if offered): Sylvie says she would prefer not to have one today. Tell the candidate it is not performed today.

check.x: Professionalism

Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Sylvie's identity, explains the purpose of the consultation, and gains consent for the examination (offering a chaperone for any intimate examination).
Is empathic and uses plain language: acknowledges how the tiredness is affecting her study, asks about periods sensitively, and does not judge her diet.
History
Characterises the fatigue:

kids.x: Onset and course: gradual over 2 to 3 months, worse in recent weeks.
Not relieved by sleep, and worse with any activity.
Impact: cannot concentrate in tutorials or study, has stopped exercising.

check.x: Asks about symptoms of anaemia:

kids.x: Palpitations: regular, fast thumping on exertion such as stairs.
Breathlessness: on stairs, and in recent weeks when walking; never before.
Dizziness: light-headed on standing, with no vertigo, imbalance or fainting.
Leg cramps when walking and always-cold hands and feet.

check.x: Takes a menstrual history:

kids.x: Cycle every 28 days. Now 8 days, previously 5. LMP last Tuesday. Menarche at 12.
Quantifies the loss: pads and tampons changed every 2 hours, changes overnight, flooding on day 1, frequent large clots.
Pain (quite bad, takes Ponstan) and premenstrual symptoms (headache, mood swings).

check.x: Asks about other sources of blood loss: melaena or rectal bleeding, other GI symptoms, haematuria, and blood donation [none; no donation for years].
Screens for a bleeding disorder: easy bruising, nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy bleeding after cuts, dental work or surgery, and family history of bleeding disorders [none].
Screens for other causes of fatigue:

kids.x: Constitutional, infective and thyroid symptoms: weight or appetite change, sweats, cough, coryza, travel, cold intolerance [only cold hands and feet].
Mood, sleep and sleep apnoea: low mood or loss of enjoyment, snoring or witnessed apnoeas [none].

check.x: Asks about sexual activity, contraception and the possibility of pregnancy [not sexually active for over a year, no contraception].
Takes a medication and allergy history: Ponstan (mefenamic acid) during periods, Centrum multivitamin, no contraception; hayfever, no drug allergies.
Takes the past and family history: previously well; mother with osteoarthritis, father with gout; no family history of bleeding disorders, coeliac disease or bowel cancer.

Takes a social history including diet: mostly takeaway with little red meat (not vegetarian), non-smoker, no alcohol, too tired to exercise, psychology student living with flatmates and well supported.

Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it may be uni stress, is falling behind and wants her energy back; and responds to her question without dismissing stress, explaining that blood tests will look for a physical cause such as anaemia.
Examination
Asks for vital signs (HR, BP, RR, SpO2, temperature) [HR 104 regular; BP 108/68 lying, 102/64 standing with HR 116 and light-headedness; RR 16; afebrile; SpO2 99%].
check.d: Credit a lying and standing BP for her postural light-headedness; the drop is small.

check.x: Examines the hands for signs of anaemia and iron deficiency [palmar crease pallor, koilonychia, cool peripheries, no clubbing].
Examines the eyes and mouth [conjunctival pallor, angular cheilitis, atrophic glossitis, no jaundice].
Inspects the skin and hair, including for bruising and petechiae [dry skin and hair; no bruising or petechiae].
Examines the cardiovascular system [tachycardia, soft ejection systolic flow murmur at the left sternal edge, JVP not raised, no oedema, chest clear].
Examines the neck for lymphadenopathy and the thyroid [normal].
Examines the abdomen for hepatosplenomegaly and a pelvic mass [normal], and offers a pelvic examination with a chaperone or says when one would be needed.
check.d: Credit offering or explaining the pelvic examination; she declines it today.

check.x: Interpretation
FBC: Hb 86 g/L is a moderate microcytic hypochromic anaemia (MCV 68, MCH 20.5) with a raised RDW and a mild reactive thrombocytosis; white cells are normal.
Blood film: microcytes, hypochromia and pencil cells fit iron deficiency, and there are no blasts.
Iron studies: ferritin 4 µg/L (below 30) confirms iron deficiency, with low iron, high transferrin and 4% saturation; a normal CRP means the ferritin is not falsely raised by inflammation.
Other bloods: negative β-hCG, normal TSH, negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA, normal coagulation screen and normal B12 and folate.
Gives iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding, made worse by a low-iron diet, as the most likely diagnosis.
Names at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, von Willebrand disease, occult GI blood loss, haematological malignancy.
Management
Explains in plain language that she is low in iron and blood because of her heavy periods, not stress, and that it is treatable.
Replaces iron:

kids.x: Oral iron (about 100 mg elemental iron, e.g. ferrous sulfate with vitamin C), daily or on alternate days, away from tea, coffee, dairy and calcium; warns about nausea, constipation and dark stools.
IV iron infusion if oral iron is not tolerated or does not work, or if a rapid rise is needed.
kids.d: Accept IV iron as first choice if justified by moderate symptomatic anaemia with ongoing heavy loss.

kids.x: States a transfusion is not needed: she is haemodynamically stable and iron deficiency responds to iron.

check.x: Treats the heavy menstrual bleeding with shared decision-making:

kids.x: Non-hormonal: tranexamic acid during heavy days; continue mefenamic acid, which also reduces the loss.

Hormonal: levonorgestrel IUD (most effective) or combined oral contraceptive pill after checking for contraindications (migraine with aura, VTE history or family history, BP), according to her preference.
Considers a pelvic ultrasound, von Willebrand studies and gynaecology referral if treatment fails or a structural or bleeding cause is suspected.

check.x: Advises an iron-rich diet (red meat, chicken, fish, legumes, leafy greens, fortified cereals), with vitamin C to help absorption.
Continues iron for about 3 months after the Hb normalises, and checks adherence and investigates for GI loss or malabsorption if she does not respond.
Safety netting

Says to call 000 or go to ED for chest pain, severe breathlessness or fainting, or for bleeding that soaks a pad or tampon every hour for 2 hours or more, or heavy bleeding with dizziness or fainting.
Explains that iron makes stools dark (but not tarry), and that black tarry or bloody stools need same-day assessment in ED; new abdominal pain needs prompt GP review.
Arranges GP review with repeat FBC (and iron studies) in 2 to 6 weeks (earlier if she cannot tolerate the iron or is not improving), and gives written information.
check.d: Accept any review within 2 to 6 weeks; expect an Hb rise of about 20 g/L by 3 to 4 weeks.

part2.lead: Your supervisor ordered blood tests after Sylvie's last visit, and she has come back for the results. Here are her full blood count and blood film, iron studies and other blood tests.
part2.patient:
Sylvie is not part of Questions 1 to 3. She comes back into the room for Question 4 and asks these questions while the candidate explains:

  • "So it's my periods that are doing this? I thought everyone's were like that."
  • "Do I need a blood transfusion?"
  • "My friend said iron tablets made her really constipated. Do I have to take them?"

Look relieved when you hear it is treatable and that your energy should come back.

handover.label: Full blood count and blood film
handover.result: Collected 4 days ago at 09:15. Blood film: red cells microcytic and hypochromic, with anisocytosis and pencil cells. Mild thrombocytosis, likely reactive. White cells normal in number and appearance; no blasts. Consistent with iron deficiency.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 86 g/L, a moderate anaemia. Microcytic and hypochromic (MCV 68, MCH 20.5, MCHC 300) with a raised RDW 18.4 (varied cell sizes). Platelets mildly raised at 452. Normal white cells, no blasts on the film. The film shows pencil cells.
  • For Sylvie: this explains her fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations, tachycardia and flow murmur. A microcytic anaemia with a high RDW and reactive thrombocytosis is the typical picture of iron deficiency (thalassaemia trait usually gives a normal RDW and a relatively high red cell count). Normal white cells and no blasts are against a haematological malignancy.
  • What it changes: confirm iron deficiency with the iron studies. She is stable, so she does not need a transfusion.

handover.label: Iron studies, CRP, B12 and folate
handover.result: Collected 4 days ago at 09:15. Lab comment: iron studies consistent with iron deficiency.
handover.model:
• Read: ferritin 4 µg/L, far below 30. Serum iron 4 µmol/L and transferrin saturation 4% are low. Transferrin 4.0 g/L is high. CRP 2 mg/L is normal. B12 and folate are normal.
  • For Sylvie: absolute iron deficiency, with her stores used up. Ferritin rises with inflammation, but her CRP is normal, so the low value is reliable. Normal B12 and folate exclude a mixed deficiency, which matters given her takeaway diet.
  • What it changes: iron deficiency anaemia is confirmed. She needs iron replacement and treatment of the cause, which is her heavy menstrual bleeding.

handover.label: Other blood tests
handover.result: Collected 4 days ago at 09:15. Von Willebrand studies were not requested.
handover.model:
• Read: β-hCG is negative. TSH is normal. tTG-IgA is negative and total IgA is normal. PT, INR, APTT and fibrinogen are normal.
  • For Sylvie: she is not pregnant, which matters for the cause of the bleeding and before starting hormonal treatment or inserting an IUD. Hypothyroidism is excluded. Coeliac disease is unlikely, and the screen is valid because her IgA is normal. A normal coagulation screen does not exclude von Willebrand disease, but her periods were normal until about a year ago and she has no other bleeding history, so it is less likely.
  • What it changes: no other cause of fatigue or iron malabsorption has been found. Request von Willebrand studies if she develops a bleeding history or treatment fails.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Sylvie, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Sylvie now, here in general practice.
Sylvie is now back in the room. Explain the results and your plan to her, answer her questions, and tell her what to watch for and what follow-up you will arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student; Sylvie, 23, psychology student.
  • Situation: 2 to 3 months of worsening fatigue with palpitations, exertional breathlessness and light-headedness.
  • Background: heavy periods for about a year: 8 days, changes every 2 hours, overnight changes, flooding and clots. Mostly takeaway diet. No GI blood loss or bleeding history. On Ponstan; no contraception.
  • Assessment: HR 104 with a small postural drop, pallor, koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis, flow murmur. Hb 86, MCV 68, high RDW, reactive platelets, pencil cells, no blasts. Ferritin 4 with normal CRP, saturation 4%. hCG, TSH, coeliac screen and coagulation normal. Iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding.
  • Recommendation: start iron (oral, or IV if needed), treat the bleeding, repeat FBC and iron studies in 2 to 6 weeks. Would you like to review her today?

Most likely: iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding, made worse by a low-iron diet. For: heavy loss with flooding and clots, symptoms and signs of anaemia, microcytic anaemia, ferritin 4 with a normal CRP.

  • Hypothyroidism: for: fatigue, cold peripheries, dry skin, and it can itself cause heavy menstrual bleeding. Against: normal TSH.
  • Coeliac disease: for: iron deficiency. Against: no GI symptoms; tTG-IgA negative with a normal IgA.
  • Von Willebrand disease: for: heavy bleeding. Against: periods were normal until a year ago, no other bleeding history, normal coagulation screen (does not exclude it).
  • Occult GI blood loss: against: no GI symptoms or melaena, and a clear menstrual cause. Investigate if she does not respond.
  • Haematological malignancy: against: normal white cells, no blasts, no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.

1. Iron: oral iron, about 100 mg elemental daily or on alternate days (e.g. ferrous sulfate with vitamin C), away from tea, coffee, dairy and calcium. IV iron infusion if she cannot tolerate it, it does not work, or a quick rise is needed. No transfusion: she is stable.
  2. Heavy bleeding (shared decision): tranexamic acid on heavy days, and keep taking mefenamic acid. Hormonal options: LNG-IUD (most effective) or the combined pill if she has no contraindications (e.g. migraine with aura, VTE risk).
  3. Further tests if needed: pelvic ultrasound, von Willebrand studies, gynaecology referral if a structural cause is suspected or treatment fails.
  4. Diet: iron-rich foods.
  5. Review: continue iron for about 3 months after Hb normalises; look for GI loss if no response.

• Explanation: her blood is low in iron because she loses more each month than she takes in. It is not stress. Iron and treating the periods will bring her energy back over weeks.
  • Transfusion: not needed.
  • Constipation: alternate-day dosing or another preparation; an infusion if tablets fail.
  • 000 or ED: chest pain, severe breathlessness or fainting; bleeding that soaks a pad or tampon every hour for 2 hours or more, or heavy bleeding with dizziness or fainting; black tarry or bloody stools (iron makes stools dark but not tarry).
  • GP soon: tummy pain, side effects, or no improvement.
  • Follow-up: GP review with repeat FBC and iron studies in 2 to 6 weeks (earlier if side effects), plus written information.

ddx.dx: Iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding, with poor dietary iron intake
ddx.for: Eight-day periods with 2-hourly changes, flooding and clots, a takeaway diet, pallor and koilonychia, Hb 86 with MCV 68, and ferritin 4 with a normal CRP.
Fatigue, always-cold hands and feet, dry skin and hair, and heavy menstrual bleeding.
ddx.against: TSH is normal at 1.6, and she has no weight gain or goitre, so it is not contributing to her fatigue or her heavy bleeding.

ddx.for: Iron deficiency in a young woman.
ddx.against: No GI symptoms or weight loss, and tTG-IgA is negative with a normal total IgA.

ddx.dx: Von Willebrand disease or another inherited bleeding disorder
ddx.for: Heavy menstrual bleeding with flooding and clots.
ddx.against: Her periods were normal until about a year ago, she has no bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding after procedures, there is no family history, and the coagulation screen is normal (though this does not exclude it).

ddx.for: Iron deficiency anaemia, and she takes an NSAID (mefenamic acid) each month.
ddx.against: No melaena, rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or bowel change, she is 23, and heavy periods fully explain the loss.

ddx.dx: Haematological malignancy such as acute leukaemia
ddx.for: Fatigue, pallor and anaemia in a young adult.
ddx.against: White cells are normal, the film shows no blasts, the platelets are raised rather than low, and she has no bruising, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly or fevers.

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Sylvie describes her periods only when asked; a candidate who does not take a menstrual history will miss the diagnosis. If a pelvic examination is offered, Sylvie declines it today; give credit for offering it or explaining when it would be needed.

In Part 2 hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Questions 1 to 3 are a discussion with the supervising GP. For Question 4 Sylvie is back in the room, and the person playing her asks her questions while the candidate explains.

Accept oral iron or an IV iron infusion as the first choice if the candidate justifies it. Tranexamic acid, the LNG-IUD and the combined pill are all acceptable for the bleeding, provided the choice is shared with her.

A high-performing candidate links the fatigue to anaemia symptoms, quantifies the menstrual loss, excludes GI loss and a bleeding history, and asks about diet and pregnancy. They find the pallor, koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis, tachycardia and flow murmur. In Part 2 they read ferritin with the CRP, treat both the iron deficit and its cause, plan a recheck, and give specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic fatigue history without asking about periods, or diagnoses "anaemia" without naming the cause. They prescribe iron without treating the bleeding, give no plan to recheck, or give vague safety netting.
explain:
The diagnosis

Sylvie has iron deficiency anaemia caused by heavy menstrual bleeding, made worse by a low-iron takeaway diet. Fatigue that sleep does not relieve, with palpitations, exertional breathlessness, light-headedness, leg cramps and cold peripheries, points to anaemia rather than a primary sleep or mood problem. The menstrual history gives the cause. Her periods have lengthened from 5 to 8 days, and she changes pads and tampons every 2 hours, changes them overnight, floods and passes large clots. Each of these suggests heavy loss. Many young women think heavy periods are normal and will not mention them unless asked.

Causes of iron deficiency

  • Blood loss (the main cause): heavy menstrual bleeding, and GI bleeding (NSAIDs, peptic ulcer, inflammatory bowel disease, malignancy).
  • Inadequate intake: poor diet, vegan or vegetarian diet without planning.
  • Impaired absorption: coeliac disease, achlorhydria, gastric surgery.
  • Increased requirements: pregnancy, lactation, infancy and growth.

Other risk factors are hookworm and dialysis. Symptoms are fatigue, reduced concentration and pica, with palpitations and breathlessness when severe. Signs are pallor (conjunctival and palmar crease), koilonychia, angular cheilitis, atrophic glossitis, dry skin and hair, tachycardia and sometimes a flow murmur.

Interpreting the results

  • FBC: a microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a raised RDW and reactive thrombocytosis is typical of iron deficiency. The film shows microcytes and pencil cells. Thalassaemia trait gives a microcytosis with a normal RDW, a relatively high red cell count and normal ferritin. If microcytosis persists once iron is replete, request haemoglobin studies for thalassaemia trait.
  • Ferritin: the most useful single test. A ferritin below 30 µg/L indicates iron deficiency. Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so inflammation can make a normal-looking ferritin misleading. Check it alongside the CRP and, if needed, the transferrin saturation.
  • Other tests: β-hCG, TSH and coeliac serology (with total IgA) look for other causes of fatigue and iron malabsorption. A coagulation screen does not exclude von Willebrand disease. Request specific von Willebrand studies when the bleeding history suggests a disorder, for example heavy periods since menarche, other bleeding symptoms or a family history.

Depression and other causes of fatigue should be screened for in the history. They are not supported here and do not explain the blood results.

Management

Treat the cause and replace the iron.

  • Oral iron is first line: a preparation with about 100 mg elemental iron, taken daily or on alternate days, on an empty stomach or with vitamin C. Alternate-day dosing may improve absorption and reduce side effects. Avoid taking it with tea, coffee, dairy, calcium or antacids. Side effects are nausea, constipation and dark stools.
  • IV iron is used when oral iron is not tolerated or does not work, when iron is not absorbed, or when a rapid rise is needed.
  • Transfusion is not given for iron deficiency in a haemodynamically stable patient (National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
  • Response: recheck the FBC and iron studies in 2 to 6 weeks; expect the Hb to rise by about 20 g/L by 3 to 4 weeks. Continue iron for about 3 months after the Hb normalises to refill stores. If she does not respond, check adherence and look for GI loss or malabsorption.

Heavy menstrual bleeding (ACSQHC Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Clinical Care Standard; RANZCOG patient information on heavy menstrual bleeding): assess the impact on her life, check the FBC, and offer treatment by shared decision-making.

  • Non-hormonal: tranexamic acid taken only on heavy days, or an NSAID such as mefenamic acid, which also reduces loss.
  • Hormonal: the levonorgestrel IUD is the most effective medical treatment. The combined oral contraceptive pill is an alternative if she has no contraindications (e.g. migraine with aura, VTE risk).
  • Further assessment: pelvic ultrasound when a structural cause such as a polyp or fibroid is suspected or treatment fails, with gynaecology referral if a structural cause is found or medical treatment fails.

Dietary advice and a dietitian help with iron-rich foods.

Safety netting

Chest pain, severe breathlessness or fainting; bleeding that soaks a pad or tampon every hour for 2 hours or more, or heavy bleeding with dizziness or fainting; and black tarry or bloody stools need 000 or same-day assessment in ED. Iron makes stools dark but not tarry, so tarry or bloody stools suggest a new GI bleed. New abdominal pain, side effects or no improvement need prompt GP review. Arrange GP review with repeat FBC and iron studies in 2 to 6 weeks.
points: In fatigue in a young woman, always take a menstrual history: lengthening periods, changes every 2 hours, overnight changes, flooding and clots indicate heavy menstrual bleeding.
A microcytic anaemia with a raised RDW and reactive thrombocytosis suggests iron deficiency; a ferritin below 30 µg/L confirms it, interpreted alongside the CRP because inflammation raises ferritin.

Treat both the cause and the deficit: iron replacement plus treatment of the heavy bleeding (tranexamic acid, an NSAID, the levonorgestrel IUD or the combined pill once contraindications such as migraine with aura and VTE risk are excluded).
Oral iron is first line (alternate-day dosing with vitamin C may help); IV iron is for intolerance, failure or a need for rapid repletion; transfusion is not needed in a stable patient.

Recheck the FBC and iron studies in 2 to 6 weeks (expect an Hb rise of about 20 g/L by 3 to 4 weeks), continue iron for about 3 months after the Hb normalises, and look for GI loss or malabsorption if she does not respond.
A normal coagulation screen does not exclude von Willebrand disease: test for it when the bleeding history suggests a bleeding disorder.
